artiest/pyotr-tchaikovsky.text:
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840 to 1893) was a Russian Romantic composer, and the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression abroad. He trained as a civil servant, because Russia offered few opportunities for a career in music and had no real music education. When the chance arose, he entered the new conservatory in St Petersburg, from which he graduated in 1865. His Western-oriented training set him apart from the nationalist composers of The Five, with whom he had a varying relationship.

Tchaikovsky wrote some of the most popular concert and theatre music in the classical repertoire: the 1812 Overture, the First Piano Concerto, the Violin Concerto, the fantasy overture Romeo and Juliet, several symphonies, the opera Eugene Onegin and the ballets Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker. His life was marked by crises and depression. His early separation from his mother, her early death, the death of his friend Nikolai Rubinstein, his failed marriage and the end of his thirteen-year bond with his patroness Nadezhda von Meck all played a part. He kept his homosexuality private. He dedicated his Sixth Symphony to his nephew Vladimir Davydov and died suddenly at the age of 53, usually attributed to cholera.

His music remained beloved by audiences, although critics were at first divided. Tchaikovsky showed that a Russian composer could use Western orchestral music to find an emotional voice of his own. His ballets belong to the standard repertoire.
artiest/pyotr-tchaikovsky.listen: Listen to a piece from The Nutcracker or Swan Lake and notice how the melody is passed from instrument to instrument. Try to hear when the music turns soft and tender and when it builds.

artiest/q-tip.text:
Q-Tip is the stage name of Kamaal Ibn John Fareed, born Jonathan William Davis in 1970 in Harlem, New York. He grew up in St. Albans, Queens. His father came from Montserrat, his mother from Alabama. He met Phife Dawg when they were only two years old, in a church. At the age of nine he began to rap, after Phife had encouraged him to, shortly after both of them had heard Rapper's Delight by The Sugarhill Gang. In the late 1980s he began his musical career as MC and main producer of A Tribe Called Quest.

With Tribe he made influential albums that linked hip hop with jazz. In the mid-1990s he co-founded the production collective The Ummah with others. His solo debut Amplified appeared in 1999. It was followed by The Renaissance in 2008, nominated for a Grammy, and the experimental Kamaal the Abstract in 2009. He also acted in films, including Poetic Justice, and since 2015 he has hosted the radio show Abstract Radio on Apple Music 1. In 2016 he became artistic director for hip hop culture at the Kennedy Center, and since 2018 he has taught a course on jazz and hip hop at New York University. In 2024 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of A Tribe Called Quest.

Q-Tip is known as an innovator of jazz-inspired hip hop production, with philosophical and introspective lyrics. AllMusic called him the leader of a jazz-based hip hop revolution in the 1990s.
artiest/q-tip.listen: Listen to a track by A Tribe Called Quest and notice the jazzy sample beneath the beat. Try to hear how Q-Tip's calm, almost conversational voice glides over it.

artiest/q65.text:
Q65 was a beat group from The Hague, founded in 1965 by the guitarists Joop Roelofs and Frank Nuyens and the singer Wim Bieler. Bass player Peter Vink and drummer Jay Baar completed the line-up. Roelofs came up with the name: a letter and a number, after the songs Susie Q and Route 66, with 65 for the year of the band's founding. The band mainly played rhythm and blues and songs by The Kinks, The Animals and The Rolling Stones. After a performance at the De Eenhoorn ice rink, the producer Peter Koelewijn invited the group to make test recordings.

In 1966 the first single, You're the Victor, was released and reached number eleven in the Top 40. After that, Hans van Hemert took over production. The follow-up, The Life I Live, reached number five and became the group's biggest hit. For promotion the band supposedly travelled to London by rubber dinghy; when they returned to Scheveningen, thousands of fans were waiting. The debut album Revolution came out later that same year, and in 1967 World of Birds reached the top 10. Drug use and Bieler's national service put a temporary end to the group in 1968.

Q65 was known for an unpolished, raw sound, and together with The Outsiders it is counted among the most important Dutch garage bands of the 1960s. After the reunion in 1970 the music sounded more psychedelic, on albums such as Afghanistan and We're Gonna Make It. The group came up in the same Hague scene as Golden Earrings and The Motions. Readers of the magazine Lust for Life chose Revolution in 2018 as one of the best albums from the Low Countries.
artiest/q65.listen: Listen to The Life I Live and notice the difference from the neat beat music of the time: the singing is rough and the band plays the rhythm and blues with great drive. Can you hear why Q65 is called a garage band?

artiest/quarteto-novo.text:
Quarteto Novo was a Brazilian group, formed in 1966 in São Paulo. It was first called Trio Novo and consisted of Theo de Barros on bass and guitar, Heraldo do Monte on viola caipira and guitar, and Airto Moreira on percussion. The group came together to accompany the singer and songwriter Geraldo Vandré, on stage and on record. When the flautist Hermeto Pascoal joined, the name became Quarteto Novo.

In 1967 the group recorded its only album, Quarteto Novo, for Odeon. That same year it accompanied Edu Lobo in a live performance of Ponteio, which won the prize for best song at the third Festival de Música Popular Brasileira. In 1967 the album received the Troféu Imprensa for best television recording by a musical group, as well as the Troféu Roquette Pinto. In 1968 the group toured Brazil as the backing band of Vandré, who was then releasing the album Canto Geral. In 1969 it broke up. EMI reissued the album on CD in 2002 and on vinyl in 2003, and a European CD appeared in 2008.

All the members came from the north-east of Brazil, a region known for the baião, except Airto Moreira, who comes from the south. The album played a part in making the baião known throughout Brazil and then beyond. Although the style is little known outside Brazil, the album influenced songwriters in America, Britain and Europe. It also helped launch the careers of the individual members.
artiest/quarteto-novo.listen: Listen to a track by Quarteto Novo and notice the interplay of viola caipira, flute and percussion. Try to hear how the rhythm of the baião drives the music.

artiest/quatuor-ebene.text:
The Quatuor Ébène is a French string quartet from Boulogne-Billancourt, founded in 1999 at the local conservatoire. It came to international attention in 2004, when it won first prize in the string quartet category of the ARD International Music Competition, together with the audience prize and two prizes for interpretation. In 2006 the first record appeared, a live recording of three Haydn quartets. In 2009 BBC Music Magazine named the quartet Newcomer of the Year for a recording of the quartets of Ravel, Fauré and Debussy. The same record was Recording of the Year at the Classic FM Gramophone Awards. In 2010 it was Ensemble of the Year at the Victoires de la Musique Classique.

The current members are the violinists Pierre Colombet and Gabriel Le Magadure, the violist Marie Chilemme since 2017 and the cellist Yuya Okamoto since 2024. Mathieu Herzog, Adrien Boisseau and Raphaël Merlin played in it earlier.

The quartet is known for its versatility. Besides classical and contemporary repertoire it plays jazz and crossover, such as the music from Pulp Fiction, arrangements of Beatles songs and a jazz version of Someday My Prince Will Come from Snow White. The 2010 album Fiction was named by NPR one of its fifty favourite albums of 2011. Its discography also includes Mozart, Schubert, Mendelssohn, Brazil, 'Round Midnight and Milestones: The Jazz Album. The New York Times called it a string quartet that can easily turn into a jazz band.
artiest/quatuor-ebene.listen: Listen to a jazz arrangement by the Quatuor Ébène and notice how four string players create swing and rhythm without drums or bass. Try to hear who plays the melody and who plays the accompaniment, and when.

artiest/queen.text:
Queen is a British rock band, formed in London in 1970 by Freddie Mercury on vocals and piano, Brian May on guitar and Roger Taylor on drums, joined in 1971 by the bass player John Deacon. May and Taylor had first played together in the band Smile. Mercury was a fan and encouraged them to experiment with more elaborate stage and studio techniques. He also suggested the name Queen. The debut album Queen appeared in 1973, and Queen II followed in 1974. Sheer Heart Attack in 1974 and A Night at the Opera in 1975 brought international success. The latter contains Bohemian Rhapsody, which spent nine weeks at the top of the British chart and helped popularise the music video as a form.

News of the World, from 1977, contained We Will Rock You and We Are the Champions, which became sports stadium anthems. In the early 1980s Queen was one of the biggest stadium bands in the world. Another One Bites the Dust, from The Game in 1980, became the band's best-selling single. According to many magazines, the performance at Live Aid in 1985 ranks among the best in rock history. Mercury gave his last performance with the band in August 1986 at Knebworth. He announced in 1991 that he had AIDS and died a day later. Made in Heaven was released in 1995.

The music grew out of progressive rock, hard rock and heavy metal and later became more accessible, with arena rock and pop. The group had a distinctive sound of its own, with multi-part vocal harmonies, May's guitar and theatrical compositions. That made Queen a fixture in pop history.
artiest/queen.listen: Listen to Bohemian Rhapsody and notice the alternation between ballad, opera and hard rock within a single song. Try to hear how often the style and the singing change.

artiest/queen-latifah.text:
Queen Latifah, whose real name is Dana Elaine Owens, is an American rapper, actress and singer, born in 1970. At nineteen she released her debut album All Hail the Queen, with the hit single Ladies First. Her second album, Nature of a Sista' from 1991, was released on Tommy Boy Records. The third album, Black Reign from 1993, was the first album by a solo female rapper to be certified gold by the American recording industry. It yielded the single U.N.I.T.Y., which drew attention to violence against women and to the objectification of Black female sexuality, and won a Grammy. The fourth album, Order in the Court from 1998, came out on Motown. The Dana Owens Album followed in 2004, Trav'lin' Light in 2007 and Persona in 2009.

Besides music she built a career as an actress. From 1993 to 1998 she played Khadijah James in the comedy series Living Single, and she had a leading role in the 1996 film Set It Off. For her role as Mama Morton in the 2002 film Chicago she was nominated for an Oscar. She also made a talk show of her own and appeared in films such as Hairspray and Girls Trip. For her role as the blues singer Bessie Smith in the 2015 HBO film Bessie she won an Emmy.

In 2006 she was the first hip hop artist with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and in 2026 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. She showed that rap could have a female, self-assured voice, especially with songs such as Ladies First and U.N.I.T.Y.
artiest/queen-latifah.listen: Listen to U.N.I.T.Y. and notice the lyrics about respect for women and how resolutely she delivers them.

artiest/questlove.text:
Questlove, whose real name is Ahmir Khalib Thompson, is an American drummer, producer, DJ, filmmaker, music journalist and actor, born in 1971 in Philadelphia. He grew up in a musical family. His father sang as Lee Andrews in the doo-wop group Lee Andrews & the Hearts. His parents took him on tour, so he grew up behind the scenes of doo-wop shows. As a child he helped with the costumes and operated the lights. At twelve he stood in as drummer in his father's band and made his debut at Radio City Music Hall.

He is the drummer and, with Black Thought, the frontman of the hip hop band The Roots. Since 2014 that group has been the house band of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, after the same role on Late Night. He produced records for artists including Elvis Costello, Common, D'Angelo, Jill Scott, Erykah Badu, Jay-Z, Al Green and John Legend. He was a member of the Soulquarians and one of the producers of the 2015 cast album of the musical Hamilton. He co-founded the websites Okayplayer and OkayAfrica, wrote eight books, taught at New York University's Clive Davis Institute and made a podcast, Questlove Supreme. He won an Oscar, six Grammys and a BAFTA.

Questlove shows how a hip hop drummer can lead a live band, with a broad musical memory ranging from soul to doo-wop. His work connects generations of musicians.
artiest/questlove.listen: Listen to a track by The Roots and notice Questlove's drumming. Try to hear how solid and yet relaxed the groove sounds.

artiest/quincy-jones.text: Quincy Jones was born in 1933 in Chicago and grew up in Seattle, where he played the trumpet and learned to arrange. He studied at Berklee in Boston and in 1957 in Paris with Nadia Boulanger and Olivier Messiaen. His first film score was The Pawnbroker (1964) by Sidney Lumet. Among those that followed were In the Heat of the Night and In Cold Blood (both 1967) and The Italian Job (1969). Jones brought the sound of the big band and of soul to the Hollywood film. In 1968 he was the first African American with two Oscar nominations in a single year. Later he became best known as a producer, notably of Michael Jackson's Thriller and of the film The Color Purple (1985).
artiest/quincy-jones.listen: Notice the horn section and the rhythm section from jazz: blues chords, brass stabs and a walking bass give the scenes an urban, modern rhythm.

artiest/quintette-du-hot-club-de-france.text:
The Quintette du Hot Club de France was a jazz group founded in France in 1934 by the guitarist Django Reinhardt and the violinist Stéphane Grappelli. The group existed in one form or another until 1948. Its origins lay in informal jam sessions backstage at the Hôtel Claridge on the Champs-Élysées in Paris, where the two played in the summer of 1934 in a band led by the bass player Louis Vola. The concert promoters Pierre Nourry and Charles Delaunay, leaders of the Hot Club de France, an association that sought to promote appreciation of jazz, urged them to form a permanent group. When Reinhardt's brother Joseph joined as a second rhythm guitarist, the quintet was complete.

What was special was the line-up. Unlike the New Orleans groups of Louis Armstrong, this quintet had what was then a new, all-string line-up: acoustic guitar and violin carried the melody, a double bass replaced the tuba, and the rhythm guitars provided chords and rhythm. There was no drummer. The group popularised Gypsy jazz, and began recording in November 1934. At first the earliest records appeared under the name Delaunay's Jazz. Later the quintet was called Django Reinhardt et le Quintette du Hot Club de France, avec Stéphane Grappelly. Later versions sometimes had a clarinettist in place of Grappelli, or a drummer.

The critic Thom Jurek called the quintet one of the most original bands in the history of recorded jazz. It was one of the first and most important jazz groups in Europe. Minor Swing from 1937, the track featured in the course, shows how European jazz found a sound of its own.
artiest/quintette-du-hot-club-de-france.listen: Listen to Minor Swing. Notice Reinhardt's guitar and Grappelli's violin taking turns to solo, and the rhythm guitars carrying the rhythm without a drummer.

artiest/quynh-nguyen.text:
Quynh Nguyen is a Vietnamese-American classical pianist and teacher, living in New York. She was born in Hanoi and studied at the Hanoi Conservatory, the Gnessin State Musical College in Moscow, the Juilliard School, the Mannes College of Music and the Graduate Center of the City University of New York, where she earned a Doctor of Musical Arts. She has performed as a soloist and recitalist in the United States, Europe and Asia, including at Carnegie Hall, Lincoln Center and the Konzerthaus in Berlin. She has played with orchestras such as the Vietnam National Symphony Orchestra, the London Symphony Orchestra and the Seattle Symphony.

Her recordings include solo albums on Arabesque Records, The Flower of France with piano works by Germaine Tailleferre on Music & Arts, and Paul Chihara: Complete Piano Works on Naxos American Classics. The last of these includes the Concerto-Fantasy, which Chihara wrote in close collaboration with her and which she recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra under Stephen Barlow. Her album of Tailleferre stood out because it brought together solo works, transcriptions and excerpts from ballet and film music.

Nguyen is associated with the music of Mozart, Chopin, Olivier Messiaen, Paul Chihara and Tailleferre. With a Fulbright grant she studied the Eastern influences on Messiaen in France and worked with Yvonne Loriod, his second wife. She teaches at Hunter College in New York.
artiest/quynh-nguyen.listen: Listen to Paul Chihara's Concerto-Fantasy with Quynh Nguyen and notice how piano and orchestra challenge each other. Try to hear when the piano takes the lead and when the orchestra takes over.

artiest/r-carlos-nakai.text:
Raymond Carlos Nakai is an American flautist, born in 1946 in Flagstaff, Arizona, into a family of Navajo and Ute descent. His father was chairman of the Navajo Nation from 1963 to 1970. As a child he listened to tapes for his parents' Navajo radio programme, and on them he heard a recording of William Horn Cloud, a Lakota musician who played the flute. At secondary school he wanted to learn the flute, but was given a cornet instead. Later he played brass in a marching band and served two years in the United States Navy.

After a car accident he could no longer play brass, because his mouth had been damaged. In 1972 he was given a traditional cedar flute, and he taught himself to play it for the most part. His first album, Changes, appeared in 1983. He then signed with Canyon Records, which released more than thirty albums by him, including Earth Spirit (1987), Canyon Trilogy (1989) and Ancestral Voices (1992). His music consists of his own compositions for the flute, inspired by traditional Native American melodies. He collaborated with artists including William Eaton, Peter Kater, Philip Glass, Nawang Khechog, Paul Horn and Keola Beamer, and received eleven Grammy nominations.

Nakai shows how a traditional instrument found a place in the meditative, spacious music that became big from the 1980s on. His flute sounds soft and breathy, often with little accompaniment around it. He lives in Tucson, Arizona. In the course he appears with Inward Journey from 1989.
artiest/r-carlos-nakai.listen: Listen to Inward Journey. Notice the soft, breathy tone of the cedar flute and the silences between the phrases.

artiest/r-d-burman.text: Rahul Dev Burman, nicknamed Pancham, was the son of the composer S.D. Burman and first worked as his father's assistant. His breakthrough came with Teesri Manzil (1966). After that he changed the sound of Hindi film music: he blended Indian melodies with rock, funk, disco and Latin American rhythms, and sought out unusual sound sources. The singer Asha Bhosle, later his wife, sang many of his best-known songs, such as Dum Maro Dum from Hare Rama Hare Krishna (1971). For Sholay (1975) he sang Mehbooba Mehbooba himself. His last score, 1942: A Love Story, was released shortly after his death in 1994.
artiest/r-d-burman.listen: Notice the Western band instruments and electric guitars beneath an Indian vocal line, and the danceable, often Latin American rhythms.

artiest/r-e-m.text:
R.E.M. was an American rock band from Athens, in the state of Georgia. In January 1980 Michael Stipe met the guitarist Peter Buck in the record shop where Buck worked. They shared a love of Patti Smith, Television and The Velvet Underground. Through a friend they got to know the students Bill Berry and Mike Mills, who had been playing together since secondary school. That same spring the four gave their first performance, at a birthday party in an old church. Stipe picked the name at random from a dictionary.

The first single, Radio Free Europe, appeared in 1981 on a small label. After that, almost one album a year followed on I.R.S. Records: Murmur (1983), Reckoning (1984), Fables of the Reconstruction (1985), Lifes Rich Pageant (1986) and Document (1987). For a long time the band was played mainly by American college radio stations. Document brought the breakthrough: The One I Love became a hit, as did It's the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine). After the move to Warner Bros., Out of Time (1991), with Losing My Religion, and Automatic for the People (1992) became the biggest successes.

The sound of R.E.M. was recognisable by the clear, broken chords of Buck's guitar, the enigmatic lyrics and Stipe's distinctive way of singing, the countermelodies in Mills's bass lines and Berry's tight drumming. Bands such as Nirvana, Pixies and Pavement named R.E.M. as a forerunner of alternative rock. Berry left in 1997, the others carried on until the band split amicably in 2011. In this way R.E.M. showed that a band from the alternative circuit in the 1980s could reach the big pop arenas without giving up its own sound.
artiest/r-e-m.listen: Listen to It's the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine) and notice the verses, in which Stipe fires off a torrent of words and images at high speed. Hear how the chorus, by contrast, is simple and sticks in the mind.

artiest/rabindranath-tagore.text:
Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861 in Calcutta, the youngest of thirteen surviving children in a family at the forefront of the Bengal Renaissance. Literary magazines were published in the house, and both Bengali and Western classical music could be heard there. His father had dhrupad singers come to teach the children Indian classical music, and one of his brothers was a composer and playwright. Tagore was writing poems at the age of eight and at sixteen published his first serious verse under the pseudonym Bhānusiṃha.

He was a poet, writer, playwright, painter and composer, and left behind an oeuvre of some two thousand songs. His best-known works are Gitanjali, Gora and Ghare-Baire. In 1913 he became the first Indian and the first non-European to receive a Nobel Prize, the one for Literature. His songs, which Bengalis call rabindrasangeet, were lyrical and spiritual and broke with rigid classical forms. Tagore remained a critic of nationalism and opposed British rule. He founded the university Visva-Bharati.

His influence on music is exceptionally large. Two countries chose a composition of his as their national anthem: Jana Gana Mana for India and Amar Sonar Bangla for Bangladesh. The national anthem of Sri Lanka, too, was inspired by his work. This makes him perhaps the only poet whose melodies are sung daily in two nations. In a pop history that is mostly about studios and record labels, he is a reminder that a song can also carry a culture. To this day his songs are recorded and sung anew.
artiest/rabindranath-tagore.listen: Listen to a recording of Jana Gana Mana, the national anthem of India. Notice how a melody written by a poet sounds like a song that a whole country can sing together.

artiest/rachel-elkind.text:
Rachel Elkind, later Rachel Elkind-Tourre, is an American classically trained musician, producer and composer. She was born on 23 February 1939. From 1967 to 1980 she worked closely with Wendy Carlos and produced her work. She then moved to France with her husband Yves Tourre.

Her best-known production is Switched-On Bach from 1968, the album on which Carlos played pieces by Johann Sebastian Bach on a synthesizer and which became a great success. It brought the electronic sound to a wide audience and showed that a synthesizer could do more than make strange noises. Elkind led the recording sessions as producer and kept watch over the whole. Carlos herself felt that her contribution was too little recognised and called her a silent partner whose work was crucial to its success.

Elkind was also heard as a singer. Her voice was put through a vocoder on a few Carlos recordings, so that a human voice became an instrument. She is also credited as co-composer of the film music of The Shining. In 1971 she produced One Voice Many, by the rock band Michaelangelo, for Columbia Records. Her name shows how much work in pop history was done by people behind the scenes. Without a producer who combined classical training with technical insight, an album like Switched-On Bach would probably not have been so convincing.
artiest/rachel-elkind.listen: Listen to an excerpt of Switched-On Bach and notice how a synthesizer plays a melody by Bach. Can you hear that every note was built up separately?

artiest/rachel-podger.text:
Rachel Podger is a British violinist and conductor who has specialised in Baroque music. She was born on 30 May 1968 to a British father and a German mother from Hamburg. The family moved to Germany, where she attended a Steiner school. She then studied in London at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama. During her studies she co-founded the chamber groups The Palladian Ensemble and Florilegium.

Podger often leads Baroque orchestras from the violin. From 1997 to 2002 she was leader of The English Concert, and she has worked as a guest conductor with, among others, the Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment. She records mainly for Channel Classics. Well-known recordings include Bach's sonatas and partitas for solo violin from 1999, Telemann's Twelve Fantasies for Solo Violin, Vivaldi's La Stravaganza from 2003 and the complete violin sonatas of Mozart. For La Stravaganza she received an award from Gramophone magazine. Her 2018 recording of Vivaldi's Le quattro stagioni reached number one in the British classical albums chart.

She plays a violin made in Genoa in 1739. Her playing is light and lively and makes use of the playing style of the period itself. She is also a professor of Baroque violin and in 2006 founded the Brecon Baroque Festival, as well as the Mozart Music Fund for young musicians. She has shown that early music can be played in a contemporary way.
artiest/rachel-podger.listen: Listen to her recording of Vivaldi's Le quattro stagioni and notice how the violin depicts the weather and the seasons. Do you hear how the soloist and the orchestra toss the ball back and forth?

artiest/rachel-portman.text: Rachel Portman studied music at Oxford and began with music for British television and film, including Mike Leigh's Life Is Sweet (1990). She writes melodically and lightly, with plenty of woodwind, strings, piano and harp. Her music often moves in small, dancing figures. That suited the many costume dramas and literary adaptations she was asked to score. With Emma (1996) she became the first woman to win an Oscar for film music. Oscar nominations followed for The Cider House Rules (1999) and Chocolat (2000). In Never Let Me Go (2010) she wrote restrained music with solo violin and piano.
artiest/rachel-portman.listen: Notice the light, dancing figures in the woodwind and strings and the warm, simple melodies.

artiest/radio-filharmonisch-orkest.text:
The Radio Filharmonisch Orkest (Netherlands Radio Philharmonic Orchestra), RFO for short, is a Dutch symphony orchestra based in Hilversum. The combined broadcasting organisations founded it in 1945, and Albert van Raalte became its first chief conductor. The first concert took place on 7 October 1945. In the early years the orchestra played mainly in the studio for radio, but gradually more and more concerts for audiences were added. Today it regularly plays in the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam and in TivoliVredenburg in Utrecht, and it can be heard on NPO Radio 4.

The orchestra has had big names as chief conductor, including Bernard Haitink, Jean Fournet, Edo de Waart, Jaap van Zweden and Markus Stenz. Since 2019 Karina Canellakis has stood in front of the orchestra, the first woman to become chief conductor of a Dutch symphony orchestra. The programme is determined by the Muziekcentrum van de Omroep (the broadcasters' music centre) and not by the orchestra alone.

The RFO plays the standard classical repertoire and also often orchestral works that are rarely performed, from Romanticism to the present. Among other things it released albums with Wagner's orchestral arrangements of Parsifal, Tristan And Isolde and Der Ring, with Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring and with Voices of Light from 1995. It also played in productions of De Nederlandse Opera. When the government wanted to cut broadcast music in 2010, protests followed and the orchestra survived. That shows how strong its position is in Dutch musical life.
artiest/radio-filharmonisch-orkest.listen: Listen to a recording by the orchestra, for example the Parsifal arrangement for orchestra alone, and notice how the instruments take over the role of the singers. Which section takes over the melody most?

artiest/radio-sinfonie-orchester-frankfu.text:
The Radio-Sinfonie-Orchester Frankfurt is the radio orchestra of the Hessian broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk. It was founded in 1929 as the Frankfurter Rundfunk-Symphonie-Orchester and bore that name until 1950. Between 1971 and 2005 it was called the Radio-Sinfonie-Orchester Frankfurt, and after that the hr-Sinfonieorchester. For foreign tours it uses the name Frankfurt Radio Symphony. The first tour, in 1980, went to the United States.

The first conductor, Hans Rosbaud, also directed the orchestra towards new music. Composers such as Alban Berg, Arnold Schönberg, Béla Bartók, Igor Stravinsky, Anton Webern and Paul Hindemith took part in the concerts, and Schönberg wrote radio talks for the station. After the war Kurt Schröder and Winfried Zillig rebuilt the orchestra. Dean Dixon and Eliahu Inbal made it an internationally respected ensemble between 1961 and 1990. Under Inbal came the first recordings of the original versions of Bruckner's symphonies and the first digital recording of all of Mahler's symphonies, both awarded a Deutscher Schallplattenpreis.

Later chief conductors were Dmitri Kitayenko, Hugh Wolff, Paavo Järvi and Andrés Orozco-Estrada. The orchestra is regarded as one of the most important Mahler and Bruckner orchestras. It shows how a radio orchestra can ensure the preservation and performance of the classical canon, but also the early presentation of new movements.
artiest/radio-sinfonie-orchester-frankfu.listen: Listen to a recording of a Mahler symphony by this orchestra and notice the difference between the soft, chamber-music-like passages and the full orchestral outbursts. How does the orchestra build the tension?

artiest/radiohead.text:
Radiohead was founded in 1985 by pupils at Abingdon School, a school south of Oxford. The band consists of the singer Thom Yorke, guitarist and keyboard player Jonny Greenwood, his brother Colin Greenwood on bass, guitarist Ed O'Brien and drummer Philip Selway. At first the group was called On a Friday; the new name comes from a song by Talking Heads. Radiohead is important because after a guitar hit the band kept choosing a different direction, and took a large audience along with it.

The first single, Creep (1992), and the album Pablo Honey (1993) made the band known as a guitar band. After The Bends (1995) came OK Computer (1997), recorded with the producer Nigel Godrich, who has worked on every album since. Paranoid Android from that album is a suite of over six minutes in four parts, with changes of time signature. OK Computer won the Grammy for best alternative album. On Kid A (2000) the band largely abandoned the familiar rock line-up. You can hear influences of electronic music, jazz, classical music and krautrock, and an ondes Martenot, an early electronic instrument.

In October 2007 Radiohead released In Rainbows itself as a download. Buyers decided for themselves what they paid, even nothing. That experiment belongs to the story of the music industry after the CD. In 2019 the band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. The motorik beat of Neu!, which SoR describes in connection with krautrock, is one of the lines that lead to Radiohead.
artiest/radiohead.listen: Paranoid Android (1997), the example from Mixtape 4: after the calm acoustic opening, a harder section begins after about two minutes. Count along: in a few groups of bars half a beat drops out, because they are in seven-eight time.

artiest/rafael-kubelik.text:
Rafael Kubelík was a Czech conductor and composer. He was born on 29 June 1914 in Býchory, the son of the famous violinist Jan Kubelík. He learned the violin from his father and studied at the Prague Conservatory, from which he graduated in 1933. At nineteen he made his debut with the Czech Philharmonic Orchestra. In 1946 he helped found the Prague Spring festival and conducted the opening concert.

After the Communist coup of February 1948 he left Czechoslovakia. He did not want to live through another tyranny, he said, after the Nazi occupation. He fled during a trip to Britain and became a Swiss citizen in 1967. He was music director of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra from 1950 to 1953 and of the Royal Opera at Covent Garden from 1955 to 1958. In 1957 he conducted and recorded the world premiere of Berlioz's Les Troyens. From 1961 to 1979 he led the Symphonieorchester des Bayerischen Rundfunks.

Kubelík left behind a large body of recordings, including of Mahler, Dvořák, Smetana and Janáček. As a composer he wrote, in a neo-Romantic style, five operas, three symphonies, chamber music, choral works and songs. His life story shows how intertwined music and politics were in Central Europe. For many listeners he is above all the conductor who knew Czech music from the inside.
artiest/rafael-kubelik.listen: Listen to his recording of Die Moldau by Smetana and notice how the orchestra makes the river flow. Do you hear how the melody begins with small streams and grows into a broad river?

artiest/rage-against-the-machine.text:
Rage Against the Machine was an American rock band, founded in 1991 in Los Angeles. The line-up consisted of the singer Zack de la Rocha, bass player Tim Commerford, guitarist Tom Morello and drummer Brad Wilk. After the break-up of his previous band, Morello was looking for a new group and brought in Wilk. The name comes from a song that De la Rocha had earlier written for his hardcore band Inside Out. The group signed with Epic Records and, by its own account, retained artistic control.

The debut album Rage Against the Machine appeared in November 1992, with on its cover the photograph of a Vietnamese monk who burned himself to death in Saigon in 1963 in protest. The breakthrough came after performances at Lollapalooza in 1993. Evil Empire from 1996 and The Battle of Los Angeles from 1999 topped the Billboard 200. In 2000 came the covers album Renegades, after which the band split up. Reunions followed later, including at Coachella in 2007.

The music blends heavy metal, rap, punk rock and funk, with lyrics that oppose authority and capitalism. Morello plays guitar while De la Rocha raps his lyrics. The band influenced the nu metal of the late 1990s and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2023. It showed that protest music can also be heavy and danceable.
artiest/rage-against-the-machine.listen: Listen to the debut album and notice the contrast between the heavy guitar and the singer's rap. Do you hear how bass and drums lay the funk underneath?

artiest/rais-khan.text:
Ustad Rais Khan was born on 25 November 1939 in Indore, in British India, and grew up in Bombay. He came from a Rajput family in which the sitar had been played for generations, beginning with Ustad Imdad Khan, the first sitar player of the subcontinent to be recorded on disc. His father Mohammed Khan was a rudra veena player and sitarist, his mother a singer. He began at a very young age, on a sitar made from a coconut. The famous sitarist Vilayat Khan was his maternal uncle.

Rais Khan belonged to the Mewati gharana, a musical school that goes back to the Mughal era. His mother's singing and his father's veena playing resounded in his own playing, so that his sitar combined styles such as khayal, dhrupad and thumri. In 1955 he was chosen to represent India at the International Youth Festival in Warsaw. In India he also played film music for singers such as Lata Mangeshkar, Mohammed Rafi and Asha Bhosle and worked with film composers such as Khayyam and Madan Mohan. His albums include Instrumental Sitar from 1969, New Sitar from 1983 and Romantic Sound of Sitar from 1990.

In 1986 he moved to Pakistan and took Pakistani nationality. There in 2017 he received the Sitara-i-Imtiaz, the third-highest civilian honour. He died on 6 May 2017. He spoke with respect of Ravi Shankar, who in his view had introduced the sitar to the world. At his peak he himself was considered one of the greatest sitar players of all time.
artiest/rais-khan.listen: Listen to a sitar recording by Rais Khan and notice the opening, where the tempo is slow and the strings ring on for a long time. Do you hear how the playing later becomes faster and the tone seems to glide?

artiest/ralf-hutter.text:
Ralf Hütter is a German musician and composer, born in 1946 in Krefeld. He studied architecture and took classes at the conservatoire in Düsseldorf, the Robert Schumann Hochschule. There he met Florian Schneider, with whom he performed at happenings and in galleries in the late 1960s. In 1970 the two founded Kraftwerk in Düsseldorf. Hütter is the singer and keyboard player of the group and the only one who has played on every album.

Together Hütter and Schneider built their own Kling Klang Studio, where they made electronic sounds unlike the guitar music from England and America. The music became ever tighter: a fixed rhythm, short melodies and a voice that often sounds almost mechanical. Hütter saw the group as a total work of art, in which music, image, design and performances belong together. He is himself reticent in interviews and prefers to let the group speak through its work. A clear personal passion is cycling, which returns in the song Tour de France and later in the 2003 album Tour de France Soundtracks.

Through Kraftwerk, Hütter's vision carried on into synth-pop, house and techno. In the course he stands at the beginning of the chapter on electronic music, as the man who, together with Schneider, put the human as machine on the stage.
artiest/ralf-hutter.listen: Listen to Tour de France and notice the sounds of bicycle chain, gear change and breathing among the synthesizers. Do you hear how an everyday theme is turned into electronic sound?

artiest/ralph-peer.text:
Ralph Peer was an American talent scout, sound engineer, producer and music publisher, born in 1892 in Independence, Missouri. He worked first for Columbia and from 1920 for the label OKeh in New York. There he directed the recording of Crazy Blues by Mamie Smith, the first blues record made specifically for an African American audience. In 1923 he took his equipment to Atlanta and recorded musicians in hotel rooms and empty warehouses, because the Southern states had no studios. In this way he had the regional music of the South committed to record for the first time.

His best-known recordings were made in August 1927 in Bristol, on the border of Tennessee and Virginia, for Victor. In an empty warehouse he recorded, among others, Jimmie Rodgers and the Carter Family. These Bristol sessions are often regarded as the beginning of commercial country music. Peer also recorded jazz, blues and gospel, for example in New Orleans and Memphis.

He also made sure that artists received a share of the copyright royalties, in addition to the income from the records. With his publishing company Southern Music he built up a large catalogue, with work by, among others, Louis Armstrong, Hoagy Carmichael and later Buddy Holly. Peer showed that regional music could become a market of its own, and that the rights to a song were worth at least as much as the recording itself.
artiest/ralph-peer.listen: Listen to a recording by the Carter Family from Bristol, such as Bury Me under the Weeping Willow. Notice the simple accompaniment and the clear singing: you can hear how early country sounds in an improvised studio.

artiest/ralph-towner.text:
Ralph Towner was born in 1940 in Chehalis, in the American state of Washington, into a musical family. His mother gave piano lessons and his father played the trumpet. At three he could already improvise on the piano. He began as a classically trained pianist, studied in Oregon from 1958 to 1963 and took classical guitar lessons at the music academy in Vienna. In the late 1960s he joined the Consort of Paul Winter, a pioneer of world music, and played jazz in New York, strongly influenced by the pianist Bill Evans.

In 1970, together with Paul McCandless, Glen Moore and Collin Walcott, he left the Winter Consort and founded the group Oregon. In the 1970s it made influential records in which folk, Indian classical forms and free improvisation from avant-garde jazz came together. At the same time began a long relationship with the label ECM, which released almost all of his solo records, beginning with Trios / Solos in 1973. He also played on Weather Report's album I Sing the Body Electric from 1972. His album Solstice (1975), with the piece Nimbus, showed his versatility on the twelve-string guitar.

Towner played nylon-string classical guitar, twelve-string guitar and piano, and used overdubs to play several parts on one record. He did not like loud music and chose small, mostly acoustic groups in which dynamics and interplay counted. For a percussive effect he slid a matchbox between the strings. He lived in Italy from the 1990s and died in January 2026 in Rome. In the course he appears with Icarus from 1972.
artiest/ralph-towner.listen: Listen to Icarus. Notice the acoustic sound and how the music breathes and floats more than an ordinary pop song.

artiest/ralph-vaughan-williams.text: Ralph Vaughan Williams was nearly seventy when he wrote his first film music. In 1940 the conductor Muir Mathieson persuaded him to contribute to 49th Parallel (1941), a war film by Michael Powell. Documentaries followed, among other things, and The Story of a Flemish Farm (1943). His best-known film work is Scott of the Antarctic (1948). For it he used a wordless soprano, women's chorus, organ and a wind machine to depict the icy expanse. He later reworked that music into his Sinfonia antartica (1952). His film style is the same as in his symphonies: modal harmony, folk-song-like melodies and a broad string sound.
artiest/ralph-vaughan-williams.listen: Listen to the modal chords and, in Scott, to the wind machine and the wordless women's voices that evoke cold and emptiness.

artiest/ramin-djawadi.text: Ramin Djawadi (born in 1974 in Duisburg) has an Iranian father and a German mother. He studied at Berklee and began in the studio of Hans Zimmer. For Iron Man (2008) he wrote a score with hard rock guitars. He became well known through the series Game of Thrones (2011). Its opening theme is built on a repeated rhythmic motif in the cello, which follows the mechanical map in the opening images. In Westworld (2016) a player piano plays covers of pop songs, such as songs by Radiohead, as a nod to the Wild West setting. For House of the Dragon (2022) he built on his earlier themes.
artiest/ramin-djawadi.listen: Notice the short, repeated motif in the cello that keeps returning at a different pitch and so builds the tension.

artiest/ramsey-lewis.text:
Ramsey Lewis was born in 1935 in Chicago and grew up in the Cabrini-Green Homes, in a family with roots in the Deep South. His father was a church choirmaster and sent him to piano lessons when he was four. Later he studied classical music at the Chicago Musical College. That rigorous technique remained audible throughout his career, even when he had long been playing jazz.

In the 1950s he formed the Ramsey Lewis Trio with bass player Eldee Young and drummer Isaac Redd Holt. They signed with Chess Records and released their debut album in 1956. The big breakthrough came in 1965 with The 'In' Crowd, a live-recorded version of a soul hit by Dobie Gray, recorded in a nightclub in Washington. The album reached number two in the pop chart and won a Grammy. Hang On Sloopy and Wade in the Water followed, each certified as a gold single. Young and Holt left in 1966, after which Maurice White, among others, took over on bass. White later founded Earth, Wind & Fire.

Lewis made over eighty albums, from Another Voyage to Sun Goddess. His style lies between jazz, gospel, rhythm and blues and pop: short, rhythmic phrases, a bluesy touch and plenty of room for the groove. In the 1970s he often played electric piano. He also presented on radio and television and campaigned for music education in Chicago. His work showed that a jazz trio could reach the charts without letting go of its swing.
artiest/ramsey-lewis.listen: Listen to The 'In' Crowd and notice the audience in the background: you can hear that it is a live recording. Then follow how the piano plays a clear, bluesy melody over a tight rhythm from bass and drums.

artiest/randy-edelman.text:
Randy Edelman is an American musician, producer, and composer and conductor for film and television. He was born on 10 June 1947 in Paterson, New Jersey, grew up in Teaneck and studied at the Cincinnati Conservatory of Music. He then worked in New York as a pianist in Broadway orchestras.

His career began with albums and songs of his own. His first solo record, Randy Edelman, appeared in 1971, followed by, among others, Farewell Fairbanks in 1975 and If Love Is Real in 1977. Other artists recorded his songs, including The Carpenters, Barry Manilow, Dionne Warwick and Blood, Sweat & Tears. His own records found a small, loyal group of listeners in the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan. He then went to work in Los Angeles for TV and film. One of his first film scores was the one for Executive Action in 1973. In the mid-1980s he wrote the theme of the TV series MacGyver.

Edelman is best known for comedies. With the director Ivan Reitman he made, among others, Twins, Ghostbusters II and Kindergarten Cop. He also wrote music for Beethoven, My Cousin Vinny, The Last of the Mohicans, The Mask, Dragonheart and Gettysburg. His music combines orchestra and pop and is often reused in advertisements, trailers and at award ceremonies. He received two Golden Globe nominations and one for a BAFTA, twelve BMI awards and in 2004 an honorary doctorate.
artiest/randy-edelman.listen: Listen to the theme of MacGyver and notice the recognisable melody that sets an atmosphere of adventure in a few seconds. Which instruments carry that melody?

artiest/randy-newman.text: Randy Newman (born in 1943) comes from a family of film composers: his uncles Alfred, Lionel and Emil Newman all worked in Hollywood. He himself first became known as a singer-songwriter with ironic songs. He wrote his first film score as early as Cold Turkey (1971), but only with Ragtime (1981) did he break through as a film composer. For The Natural (1984) he made a heroic score with brass in the style of Copland. With Toy Story (1995) began his long collaboration with Pixar. The song You've Got a Friend in Me sounds like a relaxed piano song from the American South. He won two Oscars for best song. For Marriage Story (2019) he wrote, by contrast, small, intimate music.
artiest/randy-newman.listen: Notice the warm Americana sound: brass in broad chords, or a piano with ragtime and blues influences beneath a simple vocal line.

artiest/raoul-moretti.text:
Raoul Moretti was a French composer, born in 1893 and died in 1954. He wrote music for films and operettas and devoted himself to light music. Little about his life is recorded in the sources, but his work is known in broad outline.

His film work falls mainly in the 1930s and 1940s, the time when sound film flourished in France. He wrote music for titles such as King of the Hotel and If You Wish It from 1932, Simone Is Like That and Suburban Melody from 1933 and One Night's Secret from 1934. After that came The Hortensia Sisters and Count Obligado in 1935, Sing Anyway in 1940, Moulin Rouge in 1941 and Melody for You in 1942. He also wrote for A Woman in the Night, After the Storm and A Dog's Life, all three from 1943. The titles are given here in English as they appear in the source; the original French titles may differ.

A composer like Moretti belongs to the layer of pop history that receives little attention. He worked in the world of light music, between operetta and film, where songs were made for a broad audience. His name is less well known than those of the singers and actors who performed his music, but composers like these helped supply the repertoire of the French cinema of those years.
artiest/raoul-moretti.listen: Find a song from a French film of the 1930s or 1940s and listen to the orchestra and the singing. Notice how light and danceable the music sounds.

artiest/raphael-pichon.text:
Raphaël Pichon is a French conductor and singer, born in 1984. As a child he sang in the choir of the Petits Chanteurs de Versailles. Later he studied violin and piano in Versailles and singing and conducting at the Conservatoire de Paris. He began as a countertenor and sang under conductors such as Ton Koopman, Jordi Savall and Gustav Leonhardt. By his own account, Bach's St John Passion, which he sang as a child, changed his life.

In 2006, while still a student, he founded Ensemble Pygmalion, a choir and orchestra that plays on period instruments. The ensemble seeks out the connections between composers such as Bach and Mendelssohn, Schütz and Brahms or Rameau and Gluck, and presents the great Passions, Mozart's Requiem and Monteverdi's Vespers in a new light. His recordings of Rameau began with Dardanus in 2013 and Castor et Pollux in 2015. After that came, among others, Mozart & The Weber Sisters, Libertà! Mozart & the Opera, Matthäus-Passion in 2022, Vespro della Beata Vergine in 2023 and Mass in B minor in 2025. Pichon is also artistic director of the Pulsations festival in Bordeaux.

With his ensemble, Pichon is among the conductors who are bringing early music on period instruments back to a large audience. He plays not only Baroque but also Romantic music and compares the styles with each other.
artiest/raphael-pichon.listen: Listen to a movement from his recording of the Matthäus-Passion. Notice the interplay of choir and orchestra, which is played on period instruments.

artiest/rashied-ali.text:
Rashied Ali, born Robert Patterson, was born on 1 July 1933 in Philadelphia and died on 12 August 2009. He was an American drummer in free jazz and the avant-garde, best known for his work with John Coltrane in the last years of Coltrane's life. His mother sang with Jimmie Lunceford, and his brother Muhammad Ali was also a drummer. He began as a pianist and came to the drums by way of trumpet and trombone. After his military service he studied with Philly Joe Jones and toured with Sonny Rollins.

In 1963 he moved to New York, where he played with Bill Dixon and Paul Bley. From 1965 he recorded with Coltrane, beginning with Meditations. He also played on Interstellar Space, an album of duets from 1967, and on The Olatunji Concert, the last recording made of Coltrane. Coltrane described his playing as multidirectional rhythms. After Coltrane's death he played with Coltrane's widow Alice Coltrane. In the early 1970s he ran the loft club Ali's Alley and founded the label Survival Records.

His drumming is less a fixed pulse than a stream of sounds that moves around the soloist. Later he worked with Phalanx, with James Blood Ulmer among others, and with Jaco Pastorius. He also made records such as Duo Exchange from 1973 and Judgment Day with his own quintet. He played a major part in challenging what jazz could be.
artiest/rashied-ali.listen: Listen to Interstellar Space by John Coltrane and Rashied Ali. Notice that there are only saxophone and drums and that the drums do not give a fixed beat but continually follow and challenge the saxophone.

artiest/raspberries.text:
The Raspberries were an American pop group from Cleveland, Ohio, founded in 1970. The best-known line-up consisted of Eric Carmen on vocals, guitar, bass and piano, Wally Bryson on guitar, Dave Smalley on guitar and bass and Jim Bonfanti on drums. The group grew out of two local bands from the 1960s, The Choir and Cyrus Erie. The producer Jimmy Ienner made all four albums of the 1970s.

The albums were Raspberries and Fresh from 1972, Side 3 from 1973 and Starting Over from 1974. Well-known songs are Go All the Way, Let's Pretend, I Wanna Be with You, Tonight and Overnight Sensation (Hit Record). The group split up in 1975, after which Eric Carmen had a successful solo career. In 1999 Bryson and Smalley used the name again for an album, and in 2004 the four original members came together for a reunion tour in 2005.

The music derives from the British Invasion, especially the Beatles, the Who, the Hollies and the Small Faces. The result is pop music with strong melodies, harmonies and crisp guitars. The group wore neat, matching suits, which won it many young fans and the scorn of some critics. Even so, the Raspberries are regarded as pioneers of power pop, a style that only really blossomed after the group had stopped.
artiest/raspberries.listen: Listen to Go All the Way and notice the combination of soft vocals and hard guitars. Do you hear how the harmonies in the chorus resemble the Beatles while the guitar recalls the Who?

artiest/ravi-coltrane.text:
Ravi Coltrane is an American jazz saxophonist, born on 6 August 1965. He is the son of the saxophonist John Coltrane and the harpist Alice Coltrane and was named after the sitar player Ravi Shankar. His father died in 1967, when Ravi was not yet two years old. He grew up in Los Angeles, studied saxophone at the California Institute of the Arts in 1986 and played a great deal with Steve Coleman, who strongly influenced his musical thinking.

After more than thirty recordings as a sideman, in 1997 he recorded his first album as a leader, Moving Pictures, with drummer Jeff Watts, bass player Lonnie Plaxico and pianist Michael Cain. From the Round Box followed in 2000, Mad 6 in 2002, his first album for Sony, and In Flux in 2005. Later came Blending Times, Spirit Fiction in 2012 and In Movement in 2016. He played with Geri Allen, McCoy Tyner, Pharoah Sanders, Herbie Hancock and Carlos Santana. He is co-owner of the label RKM Music, where he produced music for, among others, Luis Perdomo and Ralph Alessi. In 2005 he played in India for the first time and met Ravi Shankar there, after whom he was named.

He plays tenor and soprano saxophone and works in small line-ups in which there is room for conversation between the instruments. His name brings the line of jazz history close: the son of one of the great innovators who sought a sound of his own, and found it.
artiest/ravi-coltrane.listen: Listen to a track from Moving Pictures or In Movement and notice how the saxophone enters into conversation with the rhythm section. Do you hear space between the notes?

artiest/ravi-shankar.text: Ravi Shankar, from Varanasi, toured as a boy with the dance company of his brother Uday and then studied the sitar for years with Allauddin Khan. He wrote the music for Satyajit Ray's Apu Trilogy and brought the Indian raga to the West, together with the violinist Yehudi Menuhin and later with George Harrison. His performance at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967 made the sitar famous with a rock audience.
artiest/ravi-shankar.listen: Listen to Raga Bhimpalasi in Monterey: the sitar begins alone and slowly, and only later does the tabla come in and the tempo pick up.

artiest/ray-brown.text:
Ray Brown was an American jazz double bass player, born on 13 October 1926 in Pittsburgh and died on 2 July 2002. As a child he took piano lessons and actually wanted to play the trombone, but his father could not afford one. When a place became free in his school's jazz orchestra, he took the double bass. A great influence was Jimmy Blanton, the bass player of Duke Ellington's orchestra.

At twenty he went to New York. There Dizzy Gillespie heard him and hired him on the spot. From 1946 to 1951 he played in Gillespie's band, together with Milt Jackson, Kenny Clarke and John Lewis. The last three later formed the Modern Jazz Quartet. He also played with Art Tatum and Charlie Parker. In 1947 he married the singer Ella Fitzgerald; they divorced in 1953 but continued to perform together. From 1951 to 1965 he was a member of the Oscar Peterson Trio, first with guitarist Barney Kessel and then Herb Ellis, later with drummer Ed Thigpen. In the 1950s he recorded a great deal as a session musician for the producer Norman Granz.

He also made albums of his own, such as Bass Hit! in 1957, This One's for Blanton! in 1975 and Soft Shoe in 1974. His playing was known for a firm, assured tone and an almost self-evident swing. Brown showed how a double bass can be the foundation of a band and at the same time a soloist.
artiest/ray-brown.listen: Listen to a recording by the Oscar Peterson Trio and notice the double bass. Do you hear how, with every note, Brown holds the beat and at the same time challenges the pianist?
